analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate prices for more brand-name drugs, sooner, with tighter price caps.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 29 Senate cosponsors, all Democrats and allied independents, but the Finance Committee never acted on it and it died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have expanded the Medicare drug price negotiation program created by the Inflation Reduction Act. Medicare would negotiate prices for 20 brand-name drugs in 2026 and 40 each year after, instead of 10, 15, and 20 in the first years. Drugs would face negotiation after 3 years on the market instead of roughly 9 years for regular drugs and 13 for biologics, and the price caps Medicare could be charged would be lowered. It also repealed the rule barring Medicare from interfering in talks between drug makers and pharmacies, freeing the government to use its bargaining power more directly.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, who would see lower out-of-pocket drug costs sooner as more expensive brand-name drugs became eligible for negotiated prices earlier in their lifespan. Taxpayers also gain, because Medicare is a public program and lower drug prices mean lower federal spending.

how_it_helps.text: Medicare would negotiate prices for 20 brand-name drugs in 2026 and 40 drugs each year thereafter, double the schedule in current law.
Drugs would become eligible for negotiation 3 years after approval, down from 7 years for drugs and 11 years for biologics, so seniors would not have to wait nearly a decade for price relief.

The ceilings on negotiated prices would be tightened, for example from 65 percent to 55 percent of the non-federal average price for some drugs and from 40 percent to 30 percent for long-monopoly drugs.

The bill repealed the noninterference clause, the provision that bars Medicare from stepping into negotiations between drug makers, pharmacies, and plan sponsors, giving the government more leverage to push prices down.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name prescription drug manufacturers, who would face more negotiated drugs, earlier negotiation, and steeper price caps, cutting into the revenues that flow from Medicare's current prices.

drawbacks.text: Drug manufacturers and their allies argue that negotiating prices earlier in a drug's life and capping prices more steeply reduces the expected return on new medicines, which could mean fewer new drugs reaching the market over time. This bill's design would have made that tradeoff sharper than current law does.

Cutting prices too early could shift revenue away from medicines in their first profitable years, the period when developers recover their costs, which is a real cost an honest supporter would have to weigh against the savings for seniors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and concrete: more drugs negotiated sooner and lower price ceilings mean direct savings for millions of Medicare beneficiaries and for the federal budget. The main cost falls on drug makers' future revenue, with a credible concern about slower investment in new medicines. On balance this is a straightforward transfer from drug industry prices to patients and taxpayers, though a reasonable critic could argue the 3-year negotiation trigger is aggressive compared with other countries' systems.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Klobuchar introduced the bill on April 20, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.
Twenty-nine senators cosponsored the bill, 27 of the 48 Senate Democrats and 2 of the 4 independents, with no Republican cosponsors.
No further action was ever recorded; the Finance Committee did not hold a markup or send the bill to the floor before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who keep the slower negotiation schedule and higher price ceilings of the original Inflation Reduction Act. Seniors and taxpayers lose the additional savings this bill would have delivered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug manufacturers keep higher Medicare prices

sides.party_line_note: All 29 cosponsors were Democrats or allied independents; no Republican signed on, and the Senate's Republican minority plus the committee's inaction were enough to bury it.

industries.note: The bill would have doubled the drugs subject to Medicare price negotiation, triggered negotiation after 3 years instead of 9 to 13, and cut the maximum price ceilings. Drug makers' Medicare revenues would fall, and their interest in keeping prices high runs directly against seniors' interest in paying less.
Biologics would have become negotiable after 3 years instead of 11, an unusually short runway to recover development costs. This is the steepest single change in the bill for the biotech segment.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and Medicare drug plans
industries.note: Repealing the noninterference clause would have let Medicare formally intervene in negotiations between manufacturers, pharmacies, and Part D plan sponsors, changing the bargaining dynamics these intermediaries currently control.
